paragraphs: This paper asks how the distribution of connections in a neural network shapes what it can learn. Motivated by measurements of brain connectivity, the authors develop a statistical mechanical theory that treats structural information as a learning constraint. For a perceptron, they derive an analytical expression for memory capacity when its weights must follow a specified distribution.

The theory relates the capacity reduction to a Wasserstein distance between the constrained weight distribution and a standard normal distribution. The authors also develop a training algorithm using optimal transport and information geometry. It learns an input-output task while satisfying the distribution constraint, with training interpreted as movement along geodesics in a space of probability distributions.

Within a parameterized family, the theory predicts an optimal weight distribution; its prediction for mammalian cortical weights lies close to experimental measurements. In a teacher-student setting, the analysis also finds benefits from adopting different prior weight distributions during learning, with distribution constraints outperforming unconstrained and sign-constrained learning. These results connect measurable network structure to learning performance within the studied perceptron models.
neurips-2022-a-theory-of-weight-distribu.tldr: A theory and training algorithm connect constraints on neural-network weight distributions to memory capacity and the use of prior knowledge.

paragraphs: Cubic regularization tackles nonconvex optimization by repeatedly solving a quadratic approximation with an added cubic penalty. Solving this inner problem can itself be expensive. One existing route uses a secular equation whose evaluation requires all eigenvalues of the Hessian, the matrix describing local curvature. Computing that full collection becomes a major bottleneck.

The authors develop two approximate secular equations that use only some Hessian eigenvalues. They analyze whether their roots exist and are unique, then bound how far those roots can lie from the root of the original equation. These bounds also control the distance between the resulting approximate optimization step and the true solution of the inner problem.

The solver uses matrix-vector products without requiring matrix inversion, making its computational structure attractive for high-dimensional problems. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report better performance than two state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a cheaper inner solver with a mathematical account of its approximation error, supporting its use in applications such as low-rank recovery and deep learning.
neurips-2022-approximate-secular-equatio.tldr: Approximate secular equations make cubic-regularization subproblems cheaper to solve while providing bounds on solution error.

paragraphs: Video action detection normally requires annotations throughout a video, making labeling expensive. This paper investigates whether carefully selected frames can supply enough supervision to train an effective detector. The central difficulty is that annotation decisions happen at the frame level, while the detection task operates over videos.

The proposed active sparse labeling framework addresses both selection and training. A frame-level scoring mechanism estimates which frames would be most informative to annotate. A new loss formulation then allows the action detector to learn from these sparse annotations. These two components work together: selecting useful frames is valuable only if the training procedure can make effective use of the incomplete labels.

On UCF-101-24 and J-HMDB-21, the authors report results better than random selection and all other evaluated baselines. Using only 10% of annotations, performance is comparable to the supervised approach. The findings show that, in these evaluations, annotation value varies enough across frames for selective labeling to substantially reduce the amount of human annotation needed.
neurips-2022-are-all-frames-equal-active.tldr: Active sparse labeling selects informative video frames and trains on their labels, reaching comparable supervised performance with 10% of annotations in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent must balance using what it knows with exploring uncertain possibilities. Optimism in the face of uncertainty encourages exploration by considering favorable possibilities that remain consistent with available evidence. In model-based reinforcement learning, implementing this idea can require a confidence set of plausible models and repeated nonlinear constrained optimization, which may be computationally intractable.

Bayesian optimistic optimization, or BOO, changes how those constraints are handled. It uses dynamic weighting to enforce the constraint rather than explicitly solving the constrained optimization problem. This preserves the goal of optimistic exploration while changing the computational procedure used to pursue it. The authors also develop techniques intended to make the optimization effective.

The paper proves sample efficiency for models in a finite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a specified mathematical class of models. That condition defines the scope of the stated theoretical guarantee. Simulation experiments find BOO competitive with existing algorithms. Together, the theory and experiments support dynamic weighting as an alternative implementation of optimism for model-based learning.
neurips-2022-bayesian-optimistic-optimiz.tldr: BOO uses dynamic weighting to implement optimistic exploration, with a sample-efficiency guarantee for a specified model class and competitive simulation results.

paragraphs: Large pretrained transformers are difficult to deploy when memory and computation are limited. Representing their weights and activations with binary values can reduce those demands, but training such restricted models is challenging. This paper studies how to improve the accuracy of fully binarized transformers enough to make the approach practically useful.

BiT combines several changes to the training and representation scheme. These include a two-set binarization method and an elastic binary activation function whose parameters are learned. It also uses successive knowledge distillation: models operating at higher precision teach students operating at lower precision. This creates a sequence of training transfers toward increasingly restrictive numerical representations.

The authors report substantially higher accuracy than previously possible for binary transformers. On the GLUE language-understanding benchmark, a fully binarized model comes within as little as 5.9% of a full-precision BERT baseline. The result indicates that coordinated changes to binarization, activations, and distillation can narrow the accuracy gap associated with extreme numerical compression, although the reported binary model still differs from its full-precision reference.
neurips-2022-bit-robustly-binarized-mult.tldr: BiT combines learned binary activations, a binarization scheme, and successive distillation to bring fully binary transformers closer to full-precision BERT accuracy.

paragraphs: Predictive coding offers an account of neural computation, but common implementations include features that have not been experimentally confirmed, such as separate value and error neurons and symmetric connections between brain regions. This paper asks whether a modified predictive-coding model can better match observed cortical organization while retaining its computational purpose.

In the linear regime, the authors constrain hidden-layer activity using an idea inspired by disentangling representations. This yields an upper bound on the predictive-coding objective. Optimizing that bound produces an algorithm reported to match the original objective's performance while admitting a biologically plausible network interpretation. Its units resemble neurons with multiple compartments and use non-Hebbian learning rules.

Because the network is derived from an objective, the authors can analyze its components and prove properties in the simplified linear setting. It learns without the one-to-one connectivity or signal multiplexing required by some earlier phenomenological models. Its parameters also have physiological interpretations, connecting mathematical quantities to cortical measurements. The contribution is a principled bridge between a learning objective and a proposed biological implementation.
neurips-2022-constrained-predictive-codi.tldr: A constrained linear predictive-coding objective yields a network with biologically interpretable components and performance matching the original objective.

paragraphs: Pretrained transformers can be adapted to many tasks, but their size and computational demands make deployment challenging. This paper targets compression during downstream fine-tuning, when an existing model is adapted for a particular application. It examines transformers across language, speech, and vision using BERT, Wav2vec2.0, and Vision Transformer models.

The approach combines 4-bit quantization with 50% fine-grained structural sparsity. Quantization reduces the precision used to represent model values, while sparsity removes part of the dense numerical structure. To make these changes work together, the authors identify critical initialization choices for quantization- and sparsity-aware fine-tuning. They also introduce zero-preserving quantizers and scheduled dropout.

The reported combination achieves 16-fold compression while maintaining model accuracy. Because the techniques are applied during fine-tuning, they can be used with pretrained models being adapted to downstream tasks. The paper describes them as hardware-friendly, making them relevant to acceleration and deployment. The central result is that substantial compression across three application domains can coexist with retained accuracy when the fine-tuning procedure accounts for both reduced precision and sparsity.
neurips-2022-deep-compression-of-pre-tra.tldr: Combining 4-bit quantization, 50% sparsity, and specialized fine-tuning achieves 16-fold compression of language, speech, and vision transformers while maintaining accuracy.

paragraphs: Tensor trains provide compact representations of arrays with many dimensions. Cross approximation constructs such representations from a small selection of tensor entries, extending an idea originally based on selected matrix rows and columns. Although the method performs well in applications, understanding the accuracy of the complete reconstructed tensor has been harder than understanding individual entries.

This paper establishes error guarantees for the entire tensor under both exact and noisy measurements. That addresses a weakness of earlier entrywise guarantees, which can become very loose when extended to the full object. The analysis also explains how the choice of sampled subtensors influences the quality of the resulting approximation.

The results show that errors from an imperfect model or noisy measurements may avoid exponential growth as tensor order increases. This is a qualified possibility, rather than a blanket guarantee for every approximation. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results. The findings help explain why cross approximation can remain useful for high-order tensors, including those used to describe quantum many-body states.
neurips-2022-error-analysis-of-tensor-tr.tldr: Whole-tensor error bounds clarify how sampling choices and measurement noise affect tensor-train cross approximation.

paragraphs: A dataset can support many models with nearly the same predictive performance, yet a learning algorithm usually returns just one. The Rashomon set collects these almost-optimal alternatives. This paper develops a technique to enumerate that entire set for sparse decision trees, giving users access to choices that a single fitted tree would conceal.

The authors represent the set in a specialized data structure that supports efficient queries and sampling. This matters because trees can express complicated interactions, making their collection of near-equivalent alternatives difficult to organize. Complete enumeration lets practitioners consider desirable model properties that may be awkward to encode in the original loss function.

The paper demonstrates three uses: assessing variable importance across almost-optimal trees, deriving sets for balanced accuracy and F1-score from a set based on accuracy, and producing sets for data subsets from a full-dataset set. These applications expand analysis from one selected model to the available alternatives. The stated advance is complete enumeration for this nonlinear discrete model class, enabling more deliberate model selection among similarly performing trees.
neurips-2022-exploring-the-whole-rashomo.tldr: The paper enumerates all almost-optimal sparse decision trees and organizes them for querying, sampling, and more deliberate model selection.

paragraphs: A static image test set makes it difficult to isolate how a classifier responds to a particular scene change. Collecting real images with controlled variations in pose, scale, lighting, or occlusion is expensive. This paper introduces Counterfactual Simulation Testing, which builds realistic synthetic scenes so models can be evaluated under specific changes to those scenes.

The framework supports questions about whether a prediction survives a different viewpoint or a partially hidden object. Using it, the authors compare convolutional networks and vision transformers under naturalistic variations. They also release a simulated dataset containing 272,000 images of everyday objects with changes in pose, scale, viewpoint, lighting, and occlusion.

The experiments provide evidence that ConvNext handles pose and scale variation better than Swin and transfers better to the simulated domain, while Swin handles partial occlusion better. Robustness improves with network scale and with the amount and variety of data across the evaluated networks. These findings reveal variation-specific differences that an overall score on a fixed test set may obscure.
neurips-2022-finding-differences-between.tldr: Controlled synthetic scene changes reveal different robustness strengths for ConvNext and Swin across pose, scale, and partial occlusion.

paragraphs: Graph self-supervised learning seeks useful representations without supervised labels. The paper identifies a tension between two common approaches: predictive learning captures local relationships but misses global similarities, while contrastive learning can push perturbed graphs too close together. That pressure may obscure differences between structurally similar graphs that have different properties.

D-SLA trains a model to recognize and measure changes to a graph. It creates several perturbations with different degrees of similarity and asks the model to distinguish original graphs from modified ones. It also uses graph edit distance to target the amount of discrepancy. The objective therefore emphasizes how much a graph has changed, alongside whether a change occurred.

The authors evaluate the learned representations on molecular property prediction, protein function prediction, and link prediction. They report that D-SLA largely outperforms relevant baselines across these tasks. The findings support learning discrepancies as a useful self-supervised signal: representations can capture graph-level relationships while retaining distinctions that may matter for subsequent predictions.
neurips-2022-graph-self-supervised-learn.tldr: D-SLA learns graph representations by distinguishing original graphs from perturbations and estimating how much each perturbation changes them.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single image becomes more challenging when training data come from different sources. Existing approaches use image-level normalization to make depth representations insensitive to changes in overall scale and offset. The paper argues that this emphasizes relationships to whole-image statistics, such as scene structure, while potentially overlooking small depth differences.

The proposed method normalizes depth representations hierarchically at multiple scales. It defines normalization contexts in two ways: through spatial information and through the distribution of depth values. This gives the learning process more localized reference contexts than a single statistic for the entire image, helping preserve fine-grained depth structure.

Experiments show improved accuracy and better retention of detail compared with previous normalization strategies. The authors report state-of-the-art results on five zero-shot transfer benchmark datasets. Those results make the normalization choice relevant beyond fitting a training source: in the reported evaluations, the learned models also transfer effectively to new datasets. The contribution centers on how depth targets are normalized to support both broad structure and finer differences.
neurips-2022-hierarchical-normalization-.tldr: Hierarchical depth normalization preserves finer depth differences and improves single-image depth estimation across five zero-shot transfer benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private hypothesis tests for detecting linear relationships and the presence of mixtures in general linear models. The aim is to preserve useful statistical inference while imposing a privacy constraint. Most proposed tests adapt the F-statistic, whose non-private form has established optimality properties in this framework.

The authors also offer a mixture test based on private nonparametric testing that is especially suitable for small datasets. For the private F-statistic, they prove convergence to the asymptotic distribution of its non-private counterpart. Consequently, its statistical power—the ability to detect an effect when one is present—also converges to that of the non-private statistic.

Monte Carlo experiments show that the tests achieve their intended significance levels and have high power. Power approaches the non-private level as sample sizes increase or the privacy-loss parameter grows, with the latter allowing weaker privacy protection. The paper also identifies cases where its tests outperform existing methods. These results connect asymptotic guarantees with empirical evidence about the privacy-inference tradeoff.
neurips-2022-hypothesis-testing-for-diff.tldr: Private hypothesis tests for linear models retain useful statistical power, with private F-statistic power converging to its non-private counterpart asymptotically.

paragraphs: Topic models discover themes in document collections, but patterns of word co-occurrence do not use all available knowledge. A domain may already have a useful hierarchy of topics. This paper develops a Bayesian generative model that incorporates such prior structure into hierarchical topic discovery, aiming to produce more coherent and interpretable topic organizations.

The proposed deep embedded topic model jointly represents documents and prior knowledge by placing words and topics in a shared space. The supplied knowledge guides discovery toward interpretable taxonomies. An extended version can also adapt the graph encoding that knowledge, allowing its structure to be adjusted to fit the target collection of documents.

This adaptation matters because a supplied hierarchy need not perfectly match the corpus being analyzed. The framework gives the prior structure an active role while permitting refinement. Experiments report effective integration of prior knowledge and improvements in both hierarchical topic discovery and document representation. The contribution connects an existing organization of domain concepts with patterns learned from text, rather than relying solely on word co-occurrence.
neurips-2022-knowledge-aware-bayesian-de.tldr: A Bayesian deep topic model combines documents with prior topic hierarchies and can adapt that knowledge structure to the target corpus.

paragraphs: Multi-scale image networks combine information at different resolutions, but those resolutions can contain different mixtures of useful detail, context, and noise. This paper argues that treating scale-specific features uniformly overlooks an important design opportunity. MSANet addresses single-image denoising by considering both the characteristics within each scale and the complementary information available across scales.

Three neural blocks divide the work. An adaptive feature block aims to retain image detail while suppressing noise. An adaptive multi-scale block expands the receptive field and aggregates information across scales, supporting features that need broader context. An adaptive fusion block samples and transfers features between scales, combining their differing characteristics from coarse to fine.

The authors evaluate MSANet on three real-noise datasets and six synthetic-noise datasets, reporting superiority over 12 comparison methods. These results support tailoring feature processing to what each scale contains. The architectural contribution is the coordination of detail preservation, contextual aggregation, and adaptive transfer, so that combining resolutions also accounts for their distinct roles in the denoising task.
neurips-2022-multi-scale-adaptive-networ.tldr: MSANet improves image denoising by adapting processing within each scale and controlling how information moves between scales.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents choosing among a finite set of actions, or arms, while sharing information through a central controller. Each agent values an arm through a weighted combination of rewards across all agents. Its best choice can therefore depend on other agents' experiences, making communication often necessary for learning.

The model covers two objectives. Pure exploration seeks to identify the best arm, while regret minimization seeks to make good choices during learning. The authors establish lower bounds on the samples needed for the first objective and on regret for the second. These bounds describe fundamental performance constraints within the proposed collaborative setting.

For pure exploration, the paper proposes a near-optimal algorithm based on phased elimination, progressively removing arms from consideration. Its sampling scheme adapts to observed data within each phase and aims to match a relaxation of the lower bound. The framework also recovers and extends earlier collaborative models, including personalized federated bandits. It provides a common way to analyze learning when agents' objectives combine individual and shared rewards.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-collaborative-.tldr: A collaborative bandit model with mixed rewards yields performance lower bounds and a near-optimal algorithm for identifying each agent's best arm.

paragraphs: Noise can help optimization move through difficult nonconvex landscapes, including escaping saddle points. Yet its usefulness raises a further question: which temporal structure of noise best supports exploration? This paper investigates noise whose increments can be correlated over time, extending the study beyond processes based on ordinary Brownian motion.

The authors analyze a continuous-time, non-Markovian process based on fractional Brownian motion. In this setting, the process has temporal dependence rather than the usual memoryless structure. They show how to discretize it into an optimization algorithm called fPGD, which generalizes the existing PGD and Anti-PGD algorithms.

The paper studies fPGD both mathematically and experimentally. It finds that the algorithm has more favorable exploration abilities than PGD and Anti-PGD in some cases. That qualification is central: the findings support potential benefits from correlated noise, without identifying a universally best noise process. The contribution broadens the design space for stochastic optimization by treating the relationship between successive noise increments as a feature that can influence exploration.
neurips-2022-on-the-theoretical-properti.tldr: The fPGD algorithm uses temporally correlated noise and shows exploration advantages over PGD and Anti-PGD in some cases.

paragraphs: Large pretrained image models offer strong representations, but collecting comparable training data for 3D vision is difficult. P2P explores using that existing 2D knowledge for point-cloud analysis. It adapts the input to a pretrained image model while keeping the image model's weights frozen, requiring relatively few trainable parameters.

Point-to-Pixel prompting transforms a point cloud into a colorful image using geometry-preserving projection and geometry-aware coloring. This conversion is optimized end to end for point-cloud tasks. The key design choice is to carry geometric information into a form that an image model can process, allowing the pretrained representation to contribute to 3D analysis.

In the reported experiments, stronger pretrained image models consistently produce better 3D performance when paired with P2P. The method reaches 89.3% accuracy on the hardest ScanObjectNN setting, surpassing conventional point-cloud models with far fewer trainable parameters. It also performs competitively on ModelNet classification and ShapeNet part segmentation. These findings support input adaptation as a practical route for transferring advances in image pretraining into point-cloud tasks.
neurips-2022-p2p-tuning-pre-trained-imag.tldr: P2P converts point clouds into geometry-aware images so frozen pretrained image models can support effective 3D analysis with few trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection often needs to identify abnormal examples even when training data contain only normal ones. This paper creates a training signal by learning small changes to normal data. A classifier then learns to distinguish unchanged examples from those altered examples, which serve as constructed abnormal data during training.

The perturbation generator and classifier are trained jointly as deep neural networks. The changes should be as small as possible while remaining recognizable to the classifier. This requirement ties the two components together: the generator produces nearby alternatives, and the classifier learns a boundary that separates them from the original normal data.

The method does not prescribe a particular shape, such as a hypersphere, for the decision boundary. The authors also report fewer hyperparameters than state-of-the-art anomaly-detection approaches. Benchmark experiments support the method's effectiveness and superiority in the evaluated comparisons. The central idea is to learn both the artificial deviations and the rule for detecting them, obtaining an anomaly boundary without requiring abnormal examples in the training dataset.
neurips-2022-perturbation-learning-based.tldr: Jointly learning small perturbations and a classifier enables anomaly detection from normal-only training data without prescribing a boundary shape.

paragraphs: When labels strongly correlate with undesirable features, a neural network may learn a shortcut instead of the intended decision rule. SelecMix addresses this by constructing augmented examples that challenge those correlations. It builds on mixup, which forms weighted combinations of training examples, and focuses on choosing informative pairs to combine.

The method selects pairs that contradict a biased association in one of two ways: matching labels with dissimilar biased features, or different labels with similar biased features. Because those features are unknown, SelecMix uses an auxiliary contrastive model to compare examples. This relies on the heuristic that networks tend to learn biased features preferentially during training.

Benchmark experiments show that the approach is effective, particularly when noisy labels make bias-conflicting examples harder to identify. Pair selection is therefore the main mechanism connecting augmentation to debiasing: the mixed examples are chosen to weaken the unwanted label-feature relationship. The method offers an alternative to augmentation approaches that depend on generative models or disentangled representations, while retaining a specific heuristic for locating the relevant biased features.
neurips-2022-selecmix-debiased-learning-.tldr: SelecMix reduces reliance on spurious correlations by mixing carefully selected example pairs that contradict biased label-feature associations.

paragraphs: Masked autoencoders learn image representations by reconstructing hidden content, but image patches do not naturally provide semantic units like words. SemMAE explores semantic parts as a possible visual counterpart. It uses those parts to organize which content is hidden, making the masking process reflect relationships within and between meaningful image regions.

The method first learns semantic parts without supervision by using and refining the multiple attention heads of a vision-transformer encoder. It then changes the masking strategy during training: initially, portions of patches within each part are hidden; later, entire parts are hidden. This progression is designed to guide learning from patterns inside parts toward relationships among parts.

Experiments report stronger image representations across several vision tasks. SemMAE achieves 84.5% fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet-1k, exceeding vanilla MAE by the reported 1.4%. It also improves semantic segmentation and fine-grained recognition, reaching state-of-the-art performance in the reported evaluations. The findings support treating mask selection as a structured learning mechanism that can incorporate semantic organization.
neurips-2022-semmae-semantic-guided-mask.tldr: SemMAE learns semantic image parts and progressively masks them to teach representations that capture both within-part patterns and between-part relationships.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language models can recognize new categories through text prompts, but prompt design affects their performance. Learning prompts from downstream training data can help while also reducing generalization to unfamiliar domains. Test-time prompt tuning addresses this tension by adapting a prompt using a single test example as it arrives.

TPT generates augmented views of that example and optimizes the prompt through entropy minimization with confidence selection. The procedure aims to produce consistent predictions across the different views. Its adaptation signal therefore comes from the current test sample, avoiding a requirement for additional task-specific training data to learn the prompt.

For natural distribution shifts, the authors report an average 3.6% improvement in CLIP's zero-shot top-1 accuracy, exceeding earlier prompt-tuning approaches that use extra task-specific data. On cross-dataset generalization involving unseen categories, TPT performs on par with state-of-the-art approaches that use additional training data. These results show that per-sample prompt adaptation can improve generalization in the evaluated settings without a separate downstream prompt-training dataset.
neurips-2022-test-time-prompt-tuning-for.tldr: TPT adapts prompts from a single test sample, improving CLIP's reported zero-shot performance under natural distribution shifts without task-specific training data.

paragraphs: Mixup creates augmented training examples by combining existing examples. Saliency-aware variants try to preserve informative content, but computing saliency can be expensive, especially for large transformers. TokenMixup uses attention to guide augmentation at the token level, aiming to maximize the saliency of the resulting collection of tokens.

The paper also introduces a variant that mixes tokens within a single example, enabling augmentation of features across scales. Both versions make the choice of what to mix central to the augmentation process. The authors report that their saliency-aware augmentation is 15 times faster than gradient-based alternatives, addressing the cost of obtaining the guidance signal.

Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet-1K show significant improvements over the baseline models while being more efficient than previous methods. The approach also reaches state-of-the-art CIFAR-100 performance among transformers trained from scratch. These findings support attention-guided token mixing as a way to obtain useful content-aware augmentation without the computational burden of the compared gradient-based saliency methods.
neurips-2022-tokenmixup-efficient-attent.tldr: TokenMixup uses attention-guided token mixing to improve transformer classification with saliency-aware augmentation reported to be 15 times faster than gradient-based methods.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image pixels, and transferring a model from synthetic images to real scenes is a challenging adaptation problem. Depth information can help connect those domains. This paper argues that existing approaches leave useful information underused when they focus on depth regression without sufficiently considering depth distributions within different categories.

The proposed method adds depth-distribution density as a supporting task for segmentation. It jointly considers segmentation, depth prediction, and depth-distribution density, using a branch balance loss to coordinate the three tasks. This makes the distribution of depths part of the learning signal alongside individual depth values and semantic categories.

The authors also introduce priors describing how pixels of different categories aggregate spatially. These priors refine the pseudo-labels used for self-training, providing another way to improve the prediction model. Experiments transferring from SYNTHIA to Cityscapes and from SYNTHIA to Mapillary support the approach's effectiveness. The contribution combines category-related depth structure with spatial information to strengthen adaptation from synthetic data to real-world segmentation.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-domain-adaptat.tldr: Depth-distribution learning, balanced multitask training, and spatially refined pseudo-labels improve synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: An interpretable surrogate model can explain a complex model by approximating its decisions. Fairwashing manipulates that explanation so an unfair underlying model appears more acceptable. This paper analyzes why such deception is difficult to avoid, identifying the unfairness of the original black-box model as an irreducible factor in the phenomenon.

The authors develop FRAUD-Detect from their theoretical analysis. It measures a divergence across subpopulation-specific fidelity measures, where fidelity concerns how closely the explanation follows the original model. Examining agreement separately for subpopulations gives the detector a signal about how the surrogate represents the underlying decisions across different groups.

Experiments find that this divergence is significantly larger for deliberately fairwashed explanations than for honest ones. The authors also report robustness against an informed adversary attempting to evade the detector. These are empirical detection results alongside a theoretical characterization of the underlying problem. Together, they show why auditing an explanation's relationship to the black-box model across subpopulations can help expose deceptive presentations of model fairness.
neurips-2022-washing-the-unwashable-on-t.tldr: FRAUD-Detect identifies fairwashed explanations by measuring differences in how faithfully they represent a black-box model across subpopulations.
